title: India Tops Global SIP Returns: 74% of 5-Year Periods Beat 8% Mark
excerpt: DSP Asset Managers' 30-year, 16-country study found India the most rewarding market for systematic investors — though recent five-year Nifty SIP returns of ~4.5% show the average hides deep swings.
body:
• The headline result: DSP Asset Managers' 30-year study across 16 countries found India the best market for SIP investors — about 74% of rolling five-year SIP periods delivered returns above 8%, the highest share anywhere, with average five-year SIP returns of 13% versus 12% for lumpsum investing.
  • India vs. the world: Over 30 years, Indian equities delivered 12% SIP returns versus 11% lumpsum in local currency (5% vs 4% in real terms). The US managed 9% SIP versus 8% lumpsum — but in Australia, France, Canada and China, lumpsum investing actually edged out SIPs.
  • What SIP investors should know right now: Recent Indian five-year returns are far weaker — ACE MF data pegs the Nifty 50's five-year SIP XIRR at about 4.5% (7-year: 8.35%), below bank FDs. The study's real takeaway is consistency, not magic: investors who stayed through weak early years almost never ended with losses, and 7 in 10 five-year SIPs rebounded to double digits. Discontinuing SIPs in a slump is the most expensive mistake — a six-month pause after two years of a ₹20,000 SIP delays a ₹1 crore goal by nearly 5 months.
  • The caveats: India's five-year SIP returns ranged from -11% to +46%, so the average hides deep drawdowns. Small-caps fared worst: nearly 30% of five-year small-cap SIP periods returned under 7%. And most investors don't actually hold long enough — as of March 2025, 81% of direct SIP assets and 67% of regular SIP assets were held for less than five years, per AMFI.

A three-decade study comparing systematic investing across the world's major equity markets has given India's mutual fund investors something to cheer about — and a reminder about why patience matters. DSP Asset Managers' NETRA analysis, using major equity indices across 16 countries, found that India stood out as the best-performing market for SIP investors, with roughly 74% of rolling five-year SIP periods delivering returns above 8%.

The study examined 30- and 5-year data and found that while SIPs don't always beat lumpsum investing on headline returns, they deliver more consistent outcomes across market cycles. Average five-year SIP returns in India were 13%, compared with 12% for lumpsum investments.

Context & Background

The numbers rest on India's long compounding story. Over the past 30 years, Indian equities delivered 12% SIP returns versus 11% lumpsum in local currency terms. Adjusted for inflation, real SIP returns stood at 5% against 4% for lumpsum — meaningful in a market where inflation has historically run higher than in developed economies.

The US also favored systematic investors: SIP returns stood at 9% against 8% for lumpsum over 30 years, with real returns of 6% versus 5%. But the study is honest about SIPs' limits. In Australia, France, Canada and China, lumpsum investing generated marginally higher returns over the long run. In China, lumpsum returns stood at 7% versus 4% for SIPs — though even there, SIPs offered better downside protection, with real SIP returns of 1% against negative territory for lumpsum in several periods.

DSP's Pragati Agarwal explained the mechanics plainly: SIPs benefit from investing across market cycles because they average out entry points and capture more units during downturns. "Markets move in cycles over long periods, and SIP benefits from investing across those cycles," she said.

"Disciplined investing through SIP helps mitigate behavioural errors and reduces the impact of poor timing decisions."

— DSP Asset Managers report

Impact & Analysis

The study's most honest finding is about dispersion. India's five-year SIP returns ranged from negative 11% to 46% — a reminder that "average 13%" is a statistical artifact spanning deep losses and spectacular bull runs. In the US, the range ran from negative 23% to 19%.

That matters because Indian investors are currently living in the left tail. ACE MF data show the Nifty 50's five-year SIP XIRR at about 4.5% — below the 6–7% many bank fixed deposits offered — with the one-year figure negative. The Nifty 50 price CAGR itself fell to roughly 5.1% by September 30, 2026, after a 6% September slide. Midcaps held up better at 14.9% over five years, but small-caps show the study's worst pattern: nearly 30% of five-year small-cap SIP periods delivered under 7%.

Separate data sharpen the picture. Share.Market by PhonePe's Q2 2026 CRISP scorecard, analyzing two decades of data, found that when a SIP started with weak or negative returns in its first two years, continuing to five years reduced the chance of a loss to zero — and in about 69% of those cases, returns rebounded into double digits. Investors who kept investing through five years after marginal 0–5% starts always ended above 5%, with nearly 72% hitting double digits. Nifty 50 TRI data from 2005 to August 2026 tell the same story: the minimum five-year SIP return was -4.4%, but nobody who stayed seven years lost money.

The uncomfortable behavioral footnote comes from AMFI: despite all the evidence, 81% of direct SIP assets and 67% of regular SIP assets were held for less than five years as of March 2025. Most investors are still quitting before the data say the payoff arrives.

Diaspora Angle

For NRIs weighing India against other markets, the study offers a framework rather than a sales pitch. India's edge in the data is nominal — high inflation eats into it, leaving real returns closer to developed-market levels — and currency depreciation adds another layer for dollar- or euro-based investors. The SPIVA India Scorecard for December 2025 adds a counterweight: 84.4% of large-cap active funds underperformed their benchmark over five years, which argues for low-cost index SIPs over fund-picking for most long-term investors.

What's Next

DSP's conclusion is deliberately unglamorous: SIPs are a behavioral tool, not a return-enhancing strategy. The investors who capture the celebrated 13% average are the ones who keep investing through the negative-11% stretches. With recent five-year returns sitting at 4.5% and fresh money pouring in at record levels — monthly SIP inflows crossed ₹31,000 crore in December 2025 — the test of this study's thesis is happening in real time. The data say the investors most likely to profit from the current slump are the ones who don't stop.
